# **Strategic Blueprint for Winning First Place in the Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon Indie Track**

## **Executive Analysis of the Hackathon Mechanics and Judging Architecture**

The Meta Global AI Developer Hackathon, hosted jointly by Meta and Cerebral Valley from October 26 to November 4, 2026, represents a premier competitive arena with a $1,000,000totalcashprizepooldistributedacrosstwodistinctdivisions:theStartupTrack($550,000) and the Indie Developer Track (\$400,000), supplemented by up to \$50,000 in community and bonus awards1. Within the Indie Developer Track—which accommodates solo builders, students, and small teams of up to four participants—the prize structure is heavily top-loaded, awarding \$150,000 for first place, \$100,000 for second place, \$75,000 for third place, \$50,000 for fourth place, and \$25,000 for fifth place2. With participation capped at 20,000 selected developers globally and project submissions due on November 4, 2026, at 9:00 PM ET (02:00 UTC on November 5\) ahead of the November 9 live finals, securing the \#1 spot requires treating the 10-day build window as an exercise in asymmetric engineering and rubric optimization1.  
A foundational distinction separates the two tracks. Whereas the Startup Track evaluates whether a product can endure production workloads for paying customers, the Indie Developer Track is explicitly judged through the lens of creativity, technical ambition, and functional reliability1. Across Stage 2 evaluations and the final judging round, every submission is scored on a 0-to-10 scale across four weighted criteria: Impact (30%), Use of Meta AI Tooling (25%), Demo Execution (25%), and Technical Depth and Execution (20%)2. Furthermore, every entry must align with one of two core problem statements: **Build for Your World**, which targets firsthand domain problems that free up human time and mental bandwidth, or **Push the Frontier**, which applies AI models to software engineering, robotics, manufacturing, energy, materials, or physical systems1.

A critical second-order implication emerges from combining the judging rubric with the API credit economics. While Impact (30%), Meta AI Tooling (25%), and Demo (25%) account for 80% of the score, those three pillars depend entirely on whether the application functions flawlessly under live evaluation2. Because every accepted participant receives \$150 in Meta Model API credits—and select participants receive an additional \$100 on Modal, \$100 on Baseten, and $25onFireworks—anindiedeveloperwhodefaultsexclusivelytomuse-wonder-1.0($4.00/Mtok input, \$20.00/Mtok output) is restricted to 7.5 million output tokens1. Conversely, routing bulk agentic development, synthetic test generation, and continuous background verification through muse-spark-1.3-contributor (\$0.10/Mtok input, \$0.002/Mtok cached input, \$0.20/Mtok output) expands that identical \$150 budget to 1.5 billion input tokens or 750 million output tokens5. Strategic allocation between Contributor mode for high-frequency loops and Standard or Wonder models for final live inference allows a solo builder to deploy an army of testing agents at virtually zero marginal cost6.

## **Empirical Patterns from Past Cerebral Valley and Meta Hackathon Winners**

An examination of hundreds of submissions and finalists across recent Cerebral Valley and Meta hackathons—including the *Llama 3 Hackathon*, *Built with Opus 4.6 & 4.7*, *Google I/O Hackathon*, *OpenEnv SF*, and *The Recursive Agents Hackathon*—reveals several structural principles that govern which indie projects advance to the winner's circle9. Foremost among these is that cross-modal reality bridging consistently defeats pure text chatbots. Every grand prize finalist translates messy physical or unstructured reality into a deterministic, interactive artifact. In the *Llama 3 Cerebral Valley Hackathon*, first place went to *OpenGlass*, which turned a \$20 hardware setup into smart glasses capable of answering questions about the wearer's visual field, while second place went to *Deb8*, an autonomous multi-agent debate arena33. In subsequent 2026 Cerebral Valley events, standout finalists included *Mobius*, which converts a static physics PDF paper into a validated, interactive physics simulator9; *SimForge*, which transforms a single photograph into a physics-ready robotics simulation via six coordinating agents31; *OmniBridge*, which autonomously reverse-engineers unknown serial hardware protocols9; and *Crusoe Forge*, a recursive agent that optimizes slow Verilog hardware designs to hit target clock speeds on Lattice ECP5 FPGAs32.  
Equally decisive is the implementation of closed-loop self-verification—often referred to as autonomous purple-teaming—which commands the Technical Depth category. Judges comprised of senior machine learning engineers and venture partners heavily penalize open-loop demos that hallucinate on edge cases34. Winning architectures embed an adversarial or verification agent directly inside the product loop, as exemplified by *Aegis*, an autonomous purple-team engine that exploits and self-hardens agents in a closed execution loop11, and *Reflex*, which monitors live execution traces to rewrite agent skill files11. Similarly, *Popcorn* paired a Chrome extension with a coding agent to verify UI changes while slashing token latency31, while *Forge Proof* combined language model synthesis with formal mathematical verification for smart contracts31.  
A third differentiator involves eliminating the "screenshot tax" in agentic workflows. As documented by builders in the Cerebral Valley project gallery, standard web and video agents capture a screenshot, ship it to a generic vision model, wait 5 to 10 seconds, burn \$0.05, and receive a rough coordinate guess on every click or frame31. By replacing slow full-frame vision guessing with **SAM 3.1**—which segments and tracks 16 objects across video frames zero-shot at 3,000 RPM via purpose-built DETR inference—an indie developer achieves real-time spatial precision that legacy vision wrappers cannot match2. Finally, winners design around the 90-second judge comprehension threshold. Empirical data from Cerebral Valley judging panels indicates that evaluators typically spend 10 to 15 minutes per project merely attempting to understand what was built, and demo videos are rarely watched beyond two to three minutes8. Winning entries such as *PeerMind*, which compresses a 6-month scientific peer-review cycle into a 90-second multi-agent interaction9, and *Ruvio*, which transforms 2D floor plans into photorealistic 3D rooms in under 15 seconds37, structure their interfaces so the transformation is visually unmistakable within the first 30 seconds of playback.

## **Five Killer Application Ideas for the Indie Developer Track**

The following five application architectures have been engineered specifically for a solo indie developer operating within the October 26 – November 4, 2026 build window1. Each concept satisfies four mandatory imperatives: high real-world impact aligned with an official theme, deep multi-model Meta AI integration (SAM 3.1, Muse Spark 1.3, Muse Wonder, Muse Code, Muse Image, Muse Voice Transcribe, and Muse Glimmer), rapid construction via Muse Code parallel git worktree agents, and autonomous, zero-human-intervention testing by AI verification agents6.  
![][image3]

### **Idea 1: KineticSim — Real-World Video to Verified Physics & Robotics Digital Twin**

#### **Impact and Problem Statement Fit (30% Weight)**

Aligned with the **Push the Frontier** theme across software, robotics, and physical systems, **KineticSim** resolves one of the most persistent bottlenecks in physical computing: constructing calibrated simulation environments1. Currently, robotics researchers, mechanical engineers, and STEM educators spend days measuring physical objects, estimating friction coefficients, and hand-coding URDF or Three.js and Matter.js scenes before a single control policy can be evaluated9. KineticSim enables a user to record a 5-second smartphone video of any real-world physical mechanism—such as a pendulum assembly, a robotic gripper picking up an irregular object, a ball rolling down an inclined plane, or a mechanical linkage—and automatically compiles that video into an interactive, mathematically calibrated browser physics simulation in under 30 seconds. The immediate beneficiaries include robotics engineers prototyping sim-to-real transfer environments, mechanical technicians diagnosing kinematic faults, and physics educators generating instant interactive laboratories from classroom demonstrations1.

#### **Creative Use of Meta AI Tooling (25% Weight)**

KineticSim orchestrates four distinct Meta AI primitives in a tight mathematical pipeline that cannot be replicated with a conventional single-model wrapper2. When a user uploads a video clip, **Muse Spark 1.3** inspects the initial keyframes to identify all active mechanical bodies and static contact surfaces, emitting concise concept prompts such as "brass pendulum bob", "pivot arm", and "inclined wooden ramp"6. Those concept strings are passed directly to **SAM 3.1** on the Meta Model API, which leverages **Object Multiplex** to segment and track up to 16 objects simultaneously across every video frame at 3,000 RPM, returning pixel-accurate masks, bounding boxes, and preserved object identities over time2. A lightweight Python service extracts the centroid coordinates ![][image4], velocity vectors, and exact collision frames from SAM 3.1's temporal masks. **Muse Wonder (muse-wonder-1.0)** then ingests these kinematic trajectories alongside the video frames to infer the underlying physical constants—including gravity scaling, mass ratios, coefficient of restitution ![][image5], and kinetic friction ![][image6]—and synthesizes an executable HTML5 Canvas, Matter.js, or Three.js simulation6. Concurrently, **Muse Image** generates clean texture sprites and background assets extracted from the segmented object masks so the digital twin visually mirrors the real-world workbench, while **Muse Code (@muse-code/sdk)** manages the iterative code compilation workspace6.

#### **Technical Depth and Agentic Build-and-Test Execution (20% Weight)**

To construct KineticSim rapidly within the 10-day window, the solo developer initializes a git repository and uses **Muse Code**'s multi-agent worktree fan-out to build the application across three parallel tracks without file collisions4. The first worktree subagent constructs the FastAPI backend that streams video frames to SAM 3.1 and computes kinematic state vectors using NumPy and SciPy2. The second worktree subagent builds the React and Vite split-screen frontend—applying Muse Code's bundled /taste playbook to enforce a high-craft scientific instrument aesthetic—rendering the real video on the left and the interactive WebGL/Canvas simulation on the right4. The third worktree subagent implements the @muse-code/sdk simulation compiler service7.  
KineticSim's centerpiece technical achievement is its **Closed-Loop Sim-to-Real Verification Agent**. Once Muse Wonder generates the initial physics simulation code, a headless **Muse Code** verification agent (muse exec) launches the generated simulation inside a headless browser, records a 5-second video of the *simulated* physics run, and feeds that synthetic video back into **SAM 3.1**6. The verification agent then computes the temporal Intersection-over-Union (![][image7]) and centroid Root Mean Square Error (![][image8]) between the real-world SAM 3.1 masks and the simulated SAM 3.1 masks across every frame ![][image9]:  
![][image10]  
Whenever ![][image11] exceeds a 5% pixel threshold, the testing agent passes the divergence trace to muse-spark-1.3-contributor (\$0.10/Mtok input), which autonomously patches the damping, mass, or restitution constants in the simulation code and re-runs the headless browser check until the simulated trajectory locks onto the real-world video5.

#### **Demo Strategy and Video Architecture (25% Weight)**

The hosted prototype should pre-load three diverse 5-second real-world videos—a double-pendulum, a bouncing elastic ball collision, and a robotic claw grasping a block—alongside a live webcam upload trigger so judges can test immediately in the browser2. In the 120-second demo video, the opening 20 seconds immediately show a real video of a mechanical ramp collision on the left half of the screen; within 12 seconds, SAM 3.1's segmentation masks lock onto the moving parts and the right half of the screen spawns a live, interactive physics simulation whose trajectories match the real video pixel-for-pixel18. From 0:20 to 0:55, the video highlights the Sim-to-Real Verification Telemetry panel showing Iteration 1 failing with an 18.4% trajectory drift, followed by the headless agent rewriting the friction coefficient in real time until Iteration 3 achieves 98.7% mask alignment. Between 0:55 and 1:30, the demonstrator drags a slider in the compiled simulation to alter gravity to Lunar (![][image12]) and inserts an obstacle with the mouse, proving the output is a true executable physics engine rather than a video filter. The final 30 seconds present a concise architectural trace of the Meta Model API pipeline (SAM 3.1 ![][image13] Muse Wonder ![][image13] Muse Code SDK ![][image13] SAM 3.1 verifier)6.

### **Idea 2: GhostQA — Zero-Selector Visual & Voice Chaos Engineering Suite for Web Apps**

#### **Impact and Problem Statement Fit (30% Weight)**

Positioned within the **Push the Frontier** software engineering theme, **GhostQA** addresses the fragility of automated end-to-end (E2E) quality assurance in an era of rapid AI-generated frontend code1. Traditional Playwright and Cypress test suites shatter whenever a developer alters a CSS class or DOM hierarchy, while first-generation vision web agents take a full screenshot, wait 5 to 10 seconds per model call, burn \$0.05 per click, and guess screen coordinates31. GhostQA eliminates brittle DOM selectors altogether. By combining zero-shot **SAM 3.1** concept segmentation with **Muse Spark 1.3** and **Muse Code**'s native computer-use capabilities, GhostQA visually perceives web and mobile interfaces at 3,000 RPM, executes multi-persona chaos testing (including voice-driven accessibility workflows), detects visual layout regressions, and autonomously opens git pull requests that repair the broken UI2. Frontend engineers, solo founders, and enterprise QA teams benefit from zero-maintenance visual testing paired with automated bug remediation11.

#### **Creative Use of Meta AI Tooling (25% Weight)**

Instead of querying brittle selectors such as page.locator('\#submit-btn-v2'), GhostQA streams the headless browser viewport directly to **SAM 3.1** with semantic concept prompts including "primary checkout button", "overlapping text collision", "broken image icon", and "loading spinner"6. SAM 3.1 returns exact pixel masks and bounding boxes in milliseconds, tracking UI drawers, modals, and animations across frames via Object Multiplex18. **Muse Spark 1.3 (muse-spark-1.3-contributor)** acts as the chaos persona brain; leveraging the \$0.10/Mtok input tier, GhostQA simultaneously orchestrates four distinct testing personas—such as an impatient rage-clicking mobile shopper, a right-to-left (RTL) localization user, an adversarial XSS and prompt-injection tester, and a hands-free voice navigator—against the target web app11. **Muse Voice Transcribe (muse-voice-transcribe-1.0)** powers the voice-accessibility persona, streaming spoken navigation commands to verify audio-driven accessibility compliance6. Whenever SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark detect a broken responsive layout, such as a checkout button clipped off-screen on a mobile viewport, **Muse Image** edits the captured frame to generate a visual specification of the corrected layout6, while **Muse Code (@muse-code/sdk)** spawns an isolated git worktree to patch the underlying CSS or React component4.

#### **Technical Depth and Agentic Build-and-Test Execution (20% Weight)**

During development, the indie builder uses **Muse Code** parallel subagents to construct the platform4. The first worktree agent builds the Playwright and WebRTC video bridge that pipes browser frames into SAM 3.1 and translates returned mask centroids into deterministic pointer and keyboard actions6. The second worktree agent builds the multi-persona orchestrator on muse-spark-1.3-contributor and wires @muse-code/sdk for automated git worktree patching7. The third worktree agent constructs the "Chaos Control Center" dashboard—refined via /taste—displaying a live 4-up video matrix of the four persona agents attacking the target web app with real-time SAM 3.1 segmentation overlays4.  
To prove a testing platform works without human intervention, GhostQA incorporates an **Autonomous Fault-Injection Mutation Loop**. The repository includes a target e-commerce web application alongside a **Chaos Mutator Agent** driven by headless muse exec7. When the verification suite starts, the Mutator Agent intentionally injects 10 realistic frontend bugs into isolated git branches—such as setting z-index: \-1 on the checkout button, breaking mobile flex-wrap, introducing an unhandled API timeout, and causing modal text overflow. GhostQA's testing agents autonomously crawl the mutated branches, use SAM 3.1 mask geometry to flag all 10 visual and functional failures without a single hardcoded DOM selector, spawn a Muse Code remediation worktree to patch the CSS and TSX files, and verify that post-patch SAM 3.1 mask visibility is 100% restored4.

#### **Demo Strategy and Video Architecture (25% Weight)**

The live deployment pairs the GhostQA Chaos Control Center with an interactive sandbox store featuring a prominent **"Inject Random CSS/Logic Bug"** button so judges can trigger a live mutation and watch GhostQA detect, segment, patch, and verify the fix in under 20 seconds2. The 120-second demo video opens (0:00–0:25) by showing a conventional Playwright script crashing instantly when a button class changes, contrasted against GhostQA's 4-panel live view where SAM 3.1 pixel masks track buttons, inputs, and modals across four concurrent browser sessions18. From 0:25 to 1:00, the video demonstrates live fault injection as a mobile viewport overflow bug pushes the "Pay Now" button half off-screen; SAM 3.1's mask clipping detector flags the exact pixel truncation while Muse Image renders the target visual repair spec6. Between 1:00 and 1:35, @muse-code/sdk spins up an isolated git worktree in the background, edits the Tailwind CSS rules, hot-reloads the preview, and re-runs the SAM 3.1 visual assertion to turn the build badge green4. The final 25 seconds display live cost telemetry demonstrating how SAM 3.1 and muse-spark-1.3-contributor execute full visual QA suites for fractions of a cent2.

### **Idea 3: ChronoLens Repair — Spatial Procedural Memory & Step-Verifier for Physical Crafts & Electronics**

#### **Impact and Problem Statement Fit (30% Weight)**

Designed for the **Build for Your World** theme, **ChronoLens Repair** attacks a tangible everyday problem: over 50 million tons of consumer electronics and household appliances become waste each year, not because they are physically irreparable, but because board-level and mechanical repair expertise is locked inside dense PDF manuals while the repairer's hands are occupied holding a screwdriver or soldering iron1. Similarly, culinary fermentation hobbyists, lab technicians, and woodworking apprentices struggle to cross-reference multi-step instructions while manipulating physical materials9. ChronoLens Repair transforms any mounted smartphone, overhead webcam, or Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses stream into a hands-free, spatially aware procedural mentor27. The system fetches live repair schematics from the web, segments every physical tool, screw, and circuit component on the workbench in real time, remembers where removed parts were placed on the table, responds to hands-free voice queries, and warns the user *before* they unscrew the wrong fastener or attach a ribbon cable backward.

#### **Creative Use of Meta AI Tooling (25% Weight)**

When a user places a broken device—such as a wireless game controller, a laptop motherboard, or an espresso machine valve—under the camera, **Muse Spark 1.3** identifies the hardware model and invokes native **Web Search Grounding ({"type": "web\_search"})** to retrieve the exact teardown sequence and pinout specifications without requiring a pre-built vector database13. **SAM 3.1** then tracks up to 16 distinct objects simultaneously across the live video feed, including "4mm Phillips screw \#1", "battery connector clip", "thermal paste tube", and "metal spudger"18. Because SAM 3.1 preserves object identity across frames via Object Multiplex, ChronoLens maintains a continuous **Spatial Part Map**: if a tiny screw rolls to the edge of the desk or gets pushed aside, the user simply asks *"Where did the heatsink screw go?"* and SAM 3.1 illuminates a high-contrast mask over its exact current coordinates18. **Muse Voice Transcribe (muse-voice-transcribe-1.0)** provides continuous, hands-free streaming speech-to-text at \$0.18/hour with custom vocabulary biasing tuned to technical component terminology ("ZIF socket", "MOSFET", "Torx T8"), automatically detecting speech turns so the user never touches a keyboard6. **Muse Image** generates clean visual step callouts whenever a text instruction is ambiguous6, and the entire spatial memory state is exposed via an MCP server compatible with **Meta AI Connectors** for seamless smart glasses integration27.

#### **Technical Depth and Agentic Build-and-Test Execution (20% Weight)**

Using **Muse Code**'s parallel git worktree fan-out, the developer divides construction across three subagents4. Subagent 1 builds the low-latency WebSocket media pipeline streaming browser audio and video frames to muse-voice-transcribe-1.0 and SAM 3.16. Subagent 2 implements the **Deterministic Procedural State Machine** powered by Muse Spark 1.3, which refuses to advance from Step ![][image14] to Step ![][image15] until SAM 3.1 verifies that the spatial mask for the required physical operation (for instance, separating the battery cable mask from the motherboard socket mask) has physically occurred16. Subagent 3 builds the augmented Heads-Up Display (HUD) frontend and the MCP connector endpoint4.  
Because physical video applications frequently fail during live judging due to variable lighting or camera angles, the developer utilizes an autonomous **Synthetic Workbench Adversary Agent** built with Muse Image, FFmpeg, and headless Muse Code (muse exec)6. The testing agent generates 20 synthetic overhead workbench video sequences simulating both correct repair workflows and common human blunders—such as reaching a metal screwdriver toward the board before disconnecting the battery, or swapping two different-length screws. The headless test runner pipes these synthetic video streams into ChronoLens and verifies that the SAM 3.1 and Muse Spark 1.3 state machine intercepts 100% of out-of-order hazardous actions while accurately tracking displaced screws across desk occlusions7.

#### **Demo Strategy and Video Architecture (25% Weight)**

The web application includes both a live webcam mode—allowing any judge to place three everyday desk items such as a pen, charging cable, and earbuds case on their desk for a live spatial tracking and assembly walkthrough—and a one-click interactive 1080p overhead laptop motherboard teardown stream2. In the 120-second demo video, the first 25 seconds show an overhead view of the motherboard as the builder says aloud, *"Starting battery replacement"*; Muse Voice Transcribe captures the command, Muse Spark 1.3 with web search pulls the teardown steps, and SAM 3.1 highlights the battery connector in green and the four retaining screws in cyan6. Between 0:25 and 0:55, the builder reaches with a metal screwdriver toward a voltage regulator *before* unplugging the battery; within 400 milliseconds, SAM 3.1 detects the tool mask intersecting the PCB while the battery mask remains seated, triggering an immediate red visual and audio alert: *"Stop\! Battery connector is still live."* From 0:55 to 1:30, the builder removes three tiny screws, places them in separate spots on a cluttered desk, and asks *"Which screw came from the top-left bracket?"*, prompting ChronoLens to replay the SAM 3.1 trajectory path and highlight the exact screw18. The final 30 seconds showcase the automated CI test suite passing 20 out of 20 synthetic workbench fault-injection videos via muse exec7.

### **Idea 4: ProtoForge — Paper-to-Silicon & Executable Hardware/Protocol Synthesizer**

#### **Impact and Problem Statement Fit (30% Weight)**

Built for the **Push the Frontier** theme across hardware engineering, robotics, and energy systems, **ProtoForge** eliminates the manual translation gap between static hardware documentation and working firmware1. Across embedded systems, clean energy grid controllers (such as battery charge/discharge schedulers), and scientific instrumentation, critical control logic is locked inside 200-page PDF component datasheets, timing waveform diagrams, and academic papers9. Translating a timing waveform diagram or a serial register table from a PDF datasheet into verified driver code and simulation harnesses typically requires weeks of manual bit-banging and logic analyzer debugging9. ProtoForge enables an engineer or researcher to drop any hardware datasheet PDF, serial protocol specification, or scientific paper into the interface and autonomously compiles a verified, bit-accurate software driver, a virtual hardware emulator, and an interactive logic-analyzer workbench in minutes.

#### **Creative Use of Meta AI Tooling (25% Weight)**

Standard optical character recognition and PDF parsers corrupt timing waveforms, pinout diagrams, and register bitfields. ProtoForge renders datasheet pages as high-resolution images and calls **SAM 3.1** on the Meta Model API to segment every timing waveform, clock edge, pinout block, and state transition diagram with pixel precision6. **Muse Wonder (muse-wonder-1.0 / Full)** then ingests the full document context (up to 1M tokens) alongside the SAM-segmented timing diagrams to synthesize both the **Virtual Device Emulator** (modeling the physical sensor, battery inverter, or chip registers) and the **Host Protocol Driver** in Python, Rust, C, or Verilog6. **Muse Code (@muse-code/sdk)** orchestrates three simultaneous subagents in isolated git worktrees—one writing the Host Driver, one writing the Virtual Device Emulator, and one writing the Adversarial Protocol Fuzzer4. Whenever a timing violation or CRC checksum error occurs during testing, **Muse Spark 1.3 (muse-spark-1.3-contributor)** drives the high-speed iterative debugging loop inside Modal serverless sandboxes (\$100 free partner credits)1.

#### **Technical Depth and Agentic Build-and-Test Execution (20% Weight)**

The solo developer uses **Muse Code** to scaffold the entire application around @muse-code/sdk and Modal execution sandboxes1. Because Muse Code was co-trained with the Muse Spark and Muse Wonder model harness from day one, multi-file tool calls and shell executions proceed cleanly across long-horizon tasks4.  
ProtoForge's architecture is inherently a self-verifying multi-agent loop. Once Worktree Agent A writes the Host Driver and Worktree Agent B writes the Device Emulator from the datasheet, **Worktree Agent C (The Adversarial Fuzzer & Waveform Verifier)** executes a rigorous two-stage verification protocol. First, Agent C injects clock jitter, dropped packets, boundary register values, and out-of-spec voltage states into the virtual communication bus connecting Agent A and Agent B. Second, the virtual bus renders a digital logic-analyzer timing waveform of the actual byte exchange between the generated driver and emulator. Agent C feeds this generated waveform image alongside the original datasheet's reference timing diagram into **SAM 3.1** and **Muse Spark 1.3** to verify that setup and hold times, clock polarity, and acknowledgment pulses visually and mathematically match the manufacturer's specification16. If any assertion fails, Agent A's driver code is autonomously patched in its isolated git worktree until 100% of fuzz tests pass4.

#### **Demo Strategy and Video Architecture (25% Weight)**

The hosted app comes pre-loaded with three challenging real-world hardware specifications—an I2C/SPI environmental telemetry sensor datasheet, a Modbus solar battery inverter manual, and a custom binary robotics actuator protocol—alongside an open PDF upload dropzone9. In the 120-second demo video, the first 20 seconds show a raw PDF datasheet dropped into ProtoForge as SAM 3.1 immediately isolates the register map tables and SPI timing waveform diagrams18. From 0:20 to 0:55, a live three-pane terminal view powered by @muse-code/sdk displays three isolated git worktree agents simultaneously writing the driver, the virtual hardware emulator, and the fuzzing suite4. Between 0:55 and 1:30, the Fuzzer Agent catches an endianness bug and a clock-phase mismatch on Test \#14; Muse Spark 1.3 inspects the virtual logic analyzer trace, patches the bit-shift operator, and passes 500 out of 500 fuzz tests16. The final 30 seconds show the demonstrator adjusting virtual temperature and voltage sliders on the synthesized sensor emulator while the generated driver parses live telemetry packets in the browser without requiring physical hardware.

### **Idea 5: LexiShield Local — Hybrid Edge-Cloud Live Negotiation & Contract Co-Pilot**

#### **Impact and Problem Statement Fit (30% Weight)**

Aligned with the **Build for Your World** theme, **LexiShield Local** protects individuals, independent contractors, patients contesting medical billing or insurance prior-authorization denials, and small business owners during live high-stakes negotiations1. Everyday negotiators routinely lose thousands of dollars because counterparties slip predatory clauses into PDF addendums or use high-pressure verbal assurances on live calls that contradict the written text9. Existing cloud-only AI wrappers fail in this scenario for two fundamental reasons: users are reluctant to upload confidential financial or medical contracts to external training servers, and standard chatbots cannot cross-reference live spoken assurances against scrolling PDF clauses quickly enough during an active conversation23. LexiShield Local resolves both barriers by uniting **Muse Glimmer (30B)** for privacy-preserving local or dedicated open-weight inference with **Muse Voice Transcribe**, **SAM 3.1**, and **Muse Spark 1.3** web search grounding—detecting contradictions between what a counterparty *says* aloud and what is *written* in the contract on screen within 1.5 seconds6.

#### **Creative Use of Meta AI Tooling (25% Weight)**

LexiShield Local showcases the full breadth of Meta's open-weight and hosted API ecosystem2. **Muse Glimmer (Muse-Glimmer-30B)**, licensed under Apache 2.0, runs the private contract vault and user context engine locally (via Ollama, llama.cpp, or vLLM, or on dedicated Baseten/Fireworks open-weight endpoints funded by hackathon partner credits)1. The system exploits Muse Glimmer's native assistant to=self private deliberation format and **speculative decoding** (drafting 8 tokens per verification step) to achieve sub-second response latency while keeping sensitive financial figures strictly inside the user's isolated security domain23. Simultaneously, **Muse Voice Transcribe (muse-voice-transcribe-1.0)** transcribes the live negotiation audio stream with automatic **speaker attribution** (cleanly separating "Counterparty" from "User") and **turn detection**6. As the counterparty scrolls through a multi-page PDF contract or pricing sheet on a shared screen, **SAM 3.1** segments and tracks specific signature blocks, fine-print footnotes, and fee tables across video frames, linking the spoken transcript directly to the visual bounding box on screen6. Whenever a counterparty makes an external factual claim—such as *"Standard statutory late fees in this jurisdiction are 18%"*—LexiShield passes an anonymized, PII-stripped query to **Muse Spark 1.3** with **Web Search Grounding ({"type": "web\_search"})** enabled, returning a live cited statutory fact-check card to the user's screen16.

#### **Technical Depth and Agentic Build-and-Test Execution (20% Weight)**

The solo builder uses **Muse Code** parallel worktrees to construct the hybrid architecture4. Worktree Agent 1 configures the Muse Glimmer 30B inference service with speculative decoding and builds a deterministic PII-stripping Sentinel broker—modeled on Meta's taint-tracking security principles—so raw names, credentials, or account numbers never leave the local domain23. Worktree Agent 2 builds the real-time audio-visual synchronization bus uniting muse-voice-transcribe-1.0 speaker turns with SAM 3.1 screen-share bounding boxes6. Worktree Agent 3 builds the whisper-coach interface (styled with /taste) that surfaces non-intrusive "Verbal-Written Contradiction" and "Suggested Counter-Script" cards4.  
To verify a live negotiation co-pilot autonomously without human actors, the developer constructs an **Adversarial Red-Team Negotiator Arena**40. A headless testing agent powered by muse-spark-1.3-contributor acts as a deceptive commercial landlord, insurance adjuster, or enterprise procurement officer13. It streams synthetic multi-speaker dialogue through Muse Voice Transcribe while simultaneously scrolling a poisoned PDF contract inside a headless browser monitored by SAM 3.1, intentionally making verbal promises that contradict Clause 14.b on page 4 (for example, stating *"There is zero early termination fee"* while scrolling past a written \$5,000 liquidated damages clause)6. The automated verification suite executes 25 adversarial negotiation episodes via muse exec and verifies that LexiShield flags 100% of verbal-vs-visual contradictions and statutory bluffs in under 2 seconds7.

#### **Demo Strategy and Video Architecture (25% Weight)**

The live web application features an interactive **"Simulated Live Negotiation \+ Screen Share"** player with three pre-loaded high-stakes scenarios—a Freelance IP Assignment Trap, a Medical Prior-Authorization Appeal, and a Commercial Lease Hidden Fee Negotiation—alongside a live microphone and PDF upload mode2. In the 120-second demo video, the opening 25 seconds show a split-screen video call where a client shares a contract screen and states aloud, *"Don't worry, you retain full ownership of your pre-existing code libraries."* Instantly, Muse Voice Transcribe attributes the quote, SAM 3.1 locks a pulsing red mask onto Section 8.2 of the shared screen video, and Muse Glimmer flashes an alert: **"VERBAL TRAP: Screen Section 8.2 assigns all background IP exclusively to Client"**6. Between 0:25 and 0:55, the counterparty claims, *"Under state law, contractor non-competes here are strictly enforceable for 24 months"*; Muse Spark 1.3 with web search grounding fires a cited rebuttal card in 1.2 seconds displaying the exact statute rendering the clause void, paired with a polite one-sentence counter-script16. From 0:55 to 1:30, the video highlights the live Sentinel privacy audit log proving that personal contract entities remained inside Muse Glimmer 30B while only sanitized statutory queries reached cloud web search23. The final 30 seconds display the Red-Team Negotiator verification dashboard completing 25 adversarial call simulations with 100% trap detection accuracy.

## **Execution Roadmap: The 10-Day Indie Sprint Protocol (Oct 26 – Nov 4, 2026\)**

Winning the \$150,000 top Indie Track prize requires disciplined execution across the 10-day window so that the final 48 hours are dedicated exclusively to autonomous verification, live stability hardening, and demo video production1.

| Sprint Phase & Dates | Primary Engineering Objective | Agentic Execution & Verification Protocol |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Phase 1: API Validation & Architecture Lock** (Oct 26 – Oct 27\) | Authenticate dev.meta.ai API keys, activate the \$150 Meta Model API credits plus Modal/Baseten/Fireworks partner credits, install Muse Code CLI (curl \-fsSL https\://dev.meta.ai/install.sh \| bash), and verify baseline latency on SAM 3.1, Muse Spark 1.3, and Muse Wonder1. | Run a smoke-test script verifying SAM 3.1 video mask outputs and muse-spark-1.3-contributor tool schemas before committing to frontend UI work3. |
| **Phase 2: Parallel Worktree Core Build** (Oct 28 – Oct 30\) | Build the core multimodal pipeline and frontend interface using **Muse Code**'s isolated git worktree fan-out (@muse-code/sdk)4. | Assign Subagent 1 to the SAM 3.1 \+ Muse Spark backend, Subagent 2 to the React/Vite UI (enforcing the /taste anti-slop playbook), and Subagent 3 to the synthetic dataset generator4. |
| **Phase 3: Autonomous Agent Test Harness** (Oct 31 – Nov 1\) | Construct the closed-loop verification agent (muse exec headless runner \+ SAM 3.1 visual mask assertions / adversarial fuzzing)7. | Execute 100+ automated test runs using muse-spark-1.3-contributor (\$0.10/Mtok input) to expose edge-case crashes and record self-healing telemetry logs for the judges5. |
| **Phase 4: Cloud Deployment & Rate-Limit Hardening** (Nov 2 – Nov 3\) | Deploy the production frontend and FastAPI/Modal backend; configure response caching and fallback routing between Muse Wonder and Muse Spark 1.3 Standard (3,000 RPM / 4M TPM)2. | Test every public URL in an incognito browser window; pre-compute deterministic fallback caches for the 3 featured sample scenarios so live judging never fails even under heavy network load2. |
| **Phase 5: High-Impact Demo Video & Early Submission** (Nov 4, Submit by 12:00 PM ET — 9 hours ahead of 9:00 PM ET cutoff) | Record and edit a crisp \<150-second public YouTube/Loom demo video and submit on the Cerebral Valley portal well before the 9:00 PM ET deadline1. | Open the first 15 seconds of the video with the live cross-modal transformation (no title slides or slow intros), dedicate 30 seconds to showing the autonomous agent test loop catching and fixing a fault, and keep all cloud endpoints live through November 91. |

## **Definitive Strategic Synthesis for First Place**

While all five architectures are engineered to score in the top tier of the Indie Developer Track, **Idea 1 (KineticSim: Real-World Video to Verified Physics & Robotics Digital Twin)** and **Idea 2 (GhostQA: Zero-Selector Visual & Voice Chaos Engineering Suite)** offer the highest probability of capturing the \#1 \$150,000 prize2. Selecting **KineticSim** maximizes immediate visual astonishment while aligning squarely with Meta's **Push the Frontier** theme1. Watching a raw smartphone video of a physical mechanism get segmented at pixel accuracy by **SAM 3.1 Object Multiplex**, compiled into an interactive browser physics simulator by **Muse Wonder**, and mathematically self-calibrated by a headless **Muse Code and SAM 3.1** trajectory-diffing agent delivers an unforgettable 15-second visual hook that no text-based or conventional retrieval submission can rival6. Conversely, selecting **GhostQA** provides the optimal path if the builder favors pure full-stack web engineering with immediate developer utility. By replacing slow, brittle DOM selectors with 3,000 RPM **SAM 3.1** zero-shot visual segmentation and proving the system's efficacy via an autonomous **Chaos Mutator and Git Worktree Auto-Patching Loop**, GhostQA directly resolves a daily engineering bottleneck experienced firsthand by every technical judge on the Cerebral Valley evaluation panel2.
